turns.zh: 我喜欢它是你的 approach 的完美例子——涌现属性、让东西涌现 vs 自上而下「这是我们在做的、这是我们在聊的」。如果有人想在公司或朋友间设这个，有什么建议？什么约束和方式让它成功？

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: Communities are all about momentum. You want to have a space too small, a time too short. If you have a big cabinet space of a lot of people in it and no one's talking, people go, "I guess this is the place where we don't talk," for whatever reason. So what you're doing is you want the smallest seed of people that you know are going to be actively engaged. So maybe there's four of you that already talk over lunch and you talk about whatever topic and it's always really interesting and generative. Cool, get that group together and do a thing. And then incrementally add people who you think are going to like that already as it currently exists. And then you need to feed it so you want to make sure that it never dies. (00:53:09): And a community with no people talking is definitely dead. A community with one person talking is already dead. You don't realize it yet. And so you're trying to maximize the chance that there's an interesting conversation even when you as the facilitator are not there. This takes some active policing by the... Like a garden has a gardener, there's somebody pruning back and saying, "Hey Jeff, just so you know, I think that came out a little bit strong to Sarah's idea and maybe next time add 'I wonder' to the front of that statement," or whatever. (00:53:35): The other thing that you do is when people reach out to you and ping you, they go, "Hey, let's think about this thing," and you go, "That's a really interesting idea. You should share that in the group." And then they do. And then you engage in the group and say, "That was really interesting," little emoji response. And people who didn't watch the interaction assume that Sarah just decided proactively to stick her neck out and share that and that it worked. And so this becomes a self-sustaining norm in the community. And it's not a secret. It's not if someone asks, "Yeah, I told Sarah to share that," but people watching don't realize that. And so it becomes a place that people do take risks and feel comfortable sharing. (00:54:07): The other thing you do is once a week or so, you want to make sure that you never propose something in the group that people go, "Eh." You always want to do a thing people go, "Yeah." So what you do is you see that if you're talking to other people, you say, "I wonder if we should have a live conversation every so often, right?" The chats were so fun, but it goes, "Would you come if I did one?" "Oh yeah, I would." "Okay, great." So now I say, "Hey, a few of us are talking. We're just going to do an experiment. We're going to have an hour-long conversation over lunch on Wednesday. Anyone in the group is free to come." (00:54:33): And then what you do is you make sure it always has quorum because if it doesn't have quorum, then the thing, it looks like the community's dead. And then what you do is you send FOMO stuff afterwards. So you say, "Here's my notes from the thing," or, "Thanks Sarah, Jeff," blah, blah, blah, blah, "or an amazing conversation. I thought the insight about," blah blah blah, "was so ridiculously amazing." So you want people who were in the group who didn't come to feel like they missed out and to come to the next one. (00:54:57): And so you're constantly creating these kinds of vibes to how to do it. You can't do it if you don't have somebody with a lot of energy. I'm typically the seed crystal for a lot of the groups I'm in to start them off because I have a lot of energy, and I like, anything that people have to say that I think is open-minded or interesting, I like building on and "yes, and"-ing and that kind of gives the foundation that it can grow. But look for the people who already roughly want it. Don't try to convince somebody who doesn't want it to want it. They will not. They will ruin the whole thing.
turns.zh: 社区全靠 momentum。你要空间太小、时间太短。如果你有个大 cabinet 空间、很多人、没人说话，大家觉得「我猜这是我们不说话的地方」。所以你要的是你知道会主动 engage 的最小种子人。也许你们四个已经在午餐时聊某个话题、总是很有趣 generative。好，把那群聚起来做个事。然后增量加你觉得会喜欢它现状的人。然后你需要喂它，确保它不死。(00:53:09)：没人说话的社区 definitely 死了。一个人说话的社区已经死了，你还没意识到。所以你试图最大化即使你作为 facilitator 不在时也有有趣对话的机会。这需要一些主动 policing。像花园有园丁，有人修剪回来说「嘿 Jeff，提醒一下，我觉得你对 Sarah 的 idea 有点太重了，也许下次加个『我想』在前面」之类的。(00:53:35)：你做的另一件事是人 reach out ping 你说「嘿，想想这个」你说「那是个有趣的 idea。你该在 group 里分享。」他们分享。你在 group 里 engage 说「那很有趣」加个 emoji 反应。没看到那个互动的人以为 Sarah 主动决定伸出脖子分享、然后它 work 了。所以这变成社区里自持续的 norm。它不是秘密。如果有人问「对，我让 Sarah 分享的」，但看的人没意识到。所以它变成大家愿意 take risk……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I just love this playbook for starting to build a little bit of community within a company. Have you written about this by the way? And if not, you should write a whole post about this.
turns.zh: 我只是爱这个在公司里开始建一点社区的 playbook。你写过这个吗？如果没写过你该写整篇 post。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: I have. It's a long essay and it's just not, you can see it in Bits and Bobs. If you gave the Bits and Bobs to Claude and said, "Please write a thing about nerd clubs and essay and the style," it would do it because there's a lot of the pieces are in there, it's just not factored out.
turns.zh: 我写过。是篇长 essay，就是没——你能在 Bits and Bobs 里看到。如果你把 Bits and Bobs 给 Claude 说「请用这种风格写篇关于 nerd club 的 essay」，它会做，因为很多 piece 在里面，只是没 factored 出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see you writing something down right now, which tells me you just articulated something in a new way that you want to say.
turns.zh: 我看到你现在在写什么，告诉我你刚用新方式 articulate 了什么你想说的。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: Yeah, that's right. That's right.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned this idea of constraints of time, and it reminds me of something that you shared in one of your Bits and Bobs around productivity. You say that if you have two hours to do a five-minute task, the effort to do that is impossible and instead you should flip that. Can you talk about this insight and how to be a little more productive?
turns.zh: 你提到时间约束这个 idea，让我想到你在某个 Bits and Bobs 里关于生产力分享的。你说如果你有两小时做五分钟的任务，做的努力是不可能的，你该翻转那个。聊聊这个洞察和怎么更高效一点？

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: Yeah, I think a lot of the trick to productivity is to play yourself like a fiddle and figure out how you work and what gives you energy and set up your day to structure it that way. So I find every time you start a task, there's an activation energy, especially a task you don't really want to do. And then when you complete it, there's a boop. There's a little burst of energy. So if you do this properly, you can get small things that are extremely easy to knock out in 10 seconds of effort, and then you do one that takes 30 seconds of effort, and then you do one that takes a longer bit of effort. But if you give it too much space, it's harder to do. So you almost want to find, "Okay, listen, I got 10 minutes. I got to do this thing where I figure out how to add, do this thing in gusto that I've been putting off. Ten minutes should be enough time to do it and structure it. So okay, right now is the only time I have to do this, to do it." (00:57:01): And another trick is I use one of my original media messages actually, one of the original public ones is about always rules are better than sometimes rules for self-control. And so if you're going to diet, "I'm going to skip lunch every day." Like holy, you haven't full thought on that at some point like a day with a big executive review, "I really need to make sure I'm well-fed before I go into this review," or something. And now you've broken the streak and now it's over. Whereas if you say a thing you know can do, "I will not have a dessert unless it would be socially awkward for me to not eat it. For example, in a small environment where somebody made homemade dessert and all of us are eating it, I'm going to..." So very clear black and white rule that you can hold on forever. (00:57:50): So for example, since the pandemic started, I've done a Peloton workout every single day since the pandemic started.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得生产力的很多 trick 是把自己像 fiddle 一样弹、figure out 你怎么 work、什么给你能量、把你的一天结构成那样。我发现每次你开始任务有个激活能，尤其你不太想做的任务。完成时有个 boop，一小股能量。所以如果你正确做，你可以让极容易 10 秒 knock out 的小事，然后做一个 30 秒的，然后做一个更长的。但如果你给它太多空间，更难做。所以你几乎想找「好，听好，我有 10 分钟。我得做这个我一直拖的 figure out 怎么加做这个的事。10 分钟应该够，结构成这样。好，现在是唯一时间，去做。」(00:57:01)：另一个 trick 是我用过的一条最早的——最早的公开 mediu 消息之一——是关于 always 规则比 sometimes 规则对自控更好。所以如果你要节食，「我每天不吃午饭」。哇，某个大高管 review 日你会想「我真的得在那 review 前吃好」，现在你断了 streak，结束了。而如果你说一个你知道能做的「我不吃甜点除非不吃会社交尴尬。比如小环境某人做了自制甜点大家都在吃，我会……」非常清晰的黑白规则，你能永远坚持。(00:57:50)：比如自疫情开始我每天做 Peloton workout。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: And now once I do start going back into the office, if I had to commute into the office, I would sometimes do a meditation to check the box for that. But if I'm not commuting and I'm not deathly sick, I've done a full workout since then. And the idea each day of is today the day of all the hundreds of days in this streak that is the worst or the hardest for me to do this thing? Is this the day? No, of course it's not. I will do it. And so that keeps you in this streak that makes it harder and harder to get out of it. And in some ways, of course you can torture yourself in an unproductive way like at a certain point maybe you should stop that streak, but I think those kinds of structuring help you get the things done you want to get done.
turns.zh: 现在我如果开始回办公室，如果我得通勤进办公室，我有时会做个冥想来打卡。但如果我不通勤、我没病得厉害，从那以后我每天都做了完整 workout。每天的想法是：今天这几百天 streak 里是不是最难做这个的一天？是今天吗？不，当然不是。我会做。所以那让你在这个 streak 里，越来越难退出。当然某种意义上你可以在不 productive 的方式折磨自己，某个点也许你该停那个 streak，但我觉得那种结构化帮你完成你想完成的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like the Seinfeld trick of productivity where you just keep track of how many days in where you've done something essentially.
turns.zh: 就像 Seinfeld 的生产力 trick：你就跟踪你连续做了多少天。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And I think people don't give those kinds of tactics enough credit because there's lots of little social tricks to yourself and others. This is when you have other people who are depending on you for something and will know that you didn't do the thing, that were so much better. So just little tricks like this help you be wildly more productive.
turns.zh: 对，exactly。我觉得大家给那种战术不够信任，因为有很多对自己和别人的小社交 trick。当有别人依赖你做某事、会知道你没做时，效果好得多。所以这种小 trick 帮你 wildly 更高效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Actually, I want to go back a little bit. I'm curious what you wrote down when we were chatting earlier that you thought was a good articulation if you're able to share, if it's interesting,
turns.zh: 其实我想回退一点。我好奇你刚在我们聊天时写下了什么你觉得是好 articulation，如果你能分享，如果有趣的话。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: I wrote down, and the reason I wrote it down is I've never... And by the way, I collect everything even once I think are maybe onto something. So I wrote down, "A community with zero people speaking is dead and a community with one person speaking doesn't yet realize it's dead," is what I wrote down.
turns.zh: 我写下了——我写下的原因是我从没……顺便我收集一切即使我觉得也许 onto 什么。所以我写下：「零人说话的社区是死的，一个人说话的社区还没意识到它已经死了。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So fun. I love this practice that you have.
turns.zh: 太好玩了。我喜欢你这个练习。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: By the way, the reason I can do it, I can type insanely quickly. And in undergrad, I wrote my thesis on the emergent power dynamics in Wikipedia's user community and I did 150 hours of interviews with different editors in Wikipedia, and I transcribed them myself. And so I got really, really, really good at I can just pipe an idea straight into my fingertips and still listen to other stuff. So that's another superpower is I've just constantly, I'm able to capture it very, very quickly. I've written notes that are at least good enough for me to clean up within the next day or two into something that's more stable.
turns.zh: 顺便，我能做的原因是我打字超快。本科时我论文写的是维基百科用户社区的涌现权力 dynamics，我做了 150 小时访谈维基百科不同编辑，我自己 transcribe。所以我变得非常非常非常擅长——我可以直接把 idea 管到指尖、同时听别的。所以那是另一个超能力：我不断能非常非常快地捕捉。我写的笔记至少够好让我在一两天内清理成更稳定的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a way you built this other than... Was it just you did it and you had to do it and you just figured out how to move fast?
turns.zh: 除了你做了、必须做、figure out 怎么快——有办法 build 这个吗？

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: I just realized later that I could type really good, really fast. I could just pipe it straight through to my fingers and it worked. And, I don't know, I don't know if I hadn't written my thesis, would I have discovered that? I don't know.
turns.zh: 我后来才意识到我能打得很快、很好。我可以直接管到手指、它 work。我不知道如果我没写论文会不会发现这个。我不知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like everything you do is on super speed, the way you think, the write and get stuff done. There's a lot.
turns.zh: 我觉得你做的一切都是超速度——你思考、写、完成的方式。很多。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: I just realized when-
turns.zh: 我后来意识到当你——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... a lot of compute.
turns.zh: ……很多计算。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: ... when you're feeling productive, you're unstoppable. And so just how can you be in your flow state as much as possible? And there's things that absolutely completely grind me to a halt, and I just make sure I invest my time in situations that don't have that characteristic. So when I work on something that I believe could work and have a big impact, I can't stop. Sometimes I'll wake up at 4:00 in the morning as I'm typically an early riser and I'm just like, "I'll write this thing." The meeting starts at 7:00 and I just think there's an idea that's really cool here and I let myself lean into those kinds of when I have the moment. (01:01:05): I also find that often if I have an idea and I just have itching to write it down, if I can write down 30 minutes and get a very rough of it in one place, now it's easier to clean it up later. But that first act of creation, I do it whenever the muse hits because it's 10 million times if it's like, "Oh, write that idea down later," you keep on delaying it, delaying it, now it's a month later. "What was the idea? How did that work again?" It's gone. And so I just try to capture the interesting insights. It's like a butterfly collector. The butterflies are going by, I try to collect them and put them in my collection as quickly as possible.
turns.zh: ——感觉高效时你 unstoppable。所以怎么让自己尽可能在 flow state？有些东西绝对完全让我停下来，我就确保把时间投资在不具有那个特性的场景。所以当我 work on 我相信能 work、有大影响的东西，我停不下来。有时我凌晨 4 点醒——我通常是早起的人——就「我要写这个。」会议 7 点开始，我就觉得这里有个很酷的 idea，我让自己 leans in 那种时刻。(01:01:05)：我也发现经常如果我有 idea、痒着写下来，如果我能写 30 分钟得到一个非常粗的在一个地方，现在更容易后来清理。但那个第一个创造行为，我在灵感来时做，因为它比「哦，后来写那个 idea」好一千万倍——你一直拖、一直拖，现在一个月后「什么 idea？怎么回事？」没了。所以我试图捕捉有趣 insight。像蝴蝶收藏家。蝴蝶飞过，我试图尽快收集、放进我的收藏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Or garden as one might describe it.
turns.zh: 或花园，某人可能这么描述。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on a quote I wanted to talk to you about. I think you described it as your life philosophy. "Do things that give you energy that you are proud of." Talk about that.
turns.zh: 这触及我想和你聊的引用。我觉得你描述为你的生活哲学：「做给你能量的事、你为之自豪的事。」聊聊那个。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: So to me, it's the combination of when you're doing something you believe in and that gives you energy, you are 10 times more productive. And you also, the effort that you are doing is its own reward. And so you are indefatigable on that topic and you go for much longer. So finding the substance of things that align with you that give you energy, then just it's like infinite energy. It's like they give an opportunity cost because it energizes you more than the opportunity cost of the time to go spend to other things. (01:02:21): And two, there are ways to give yourself energy, like for example, playing a video game, or there's any kind of mind-altering substance that might give you that like, "This gives me energy." Those are not things that I'm not saying do those. I'm saying what are the things that you'll look back and say, "I'm glad I did that. I'm proud that I did that." And if you take the perspective of a 10 years on looking back on each decision and thing that you're doing, and imagine seeing this decision played in front of 1,000 people whose opinion you care about, your family, your friends, your role models, would you be proud is a good sign of life that you're taking a broad enough perspective. (01:02:55): When you're busy and in the moment, it's so easy to say, "I just got to do this one thing that's probably not great to get this thing done. And once I do it, it's going to suck. But once I do it, it'll be fine." And then you find yourself doing it again and again and again and again and before you know it, you've lost who you want to be and you're now a husk of yourself. And so I think those two pieces lean into where you find energy, where you specifically find energy, your superpower, the thing that you intrinsically enjoy doing, and just make sure it's something that you are actively proud of and that helped make sure you don't take a bunch of shortcuts.
turns.zh: 对我来说是组合：当你做你相信的、给你能量的事，你高效 10 倍。而且你的努力本身就是回报。所以你 indefatigable，你持续更久。所以找到和你 align、给你能量的东西的 substance，然后就像无限能量。它给你能量超过花在其他事上的机会成本，所以是个机会成本。(01:02:21)：第二，有些给你能量的方式，比如打游戏，或有任何 mind-altering 物质可能给你「这给我能量」。我不是说做那些。我是说什么是你回头看会说「我很高兴我做了。我自豪我做了」的。如果你用 10 年后回看每个你在做的决策和事的视角，想象这个决策在 1000 个你在乎其意见的人——家人、朋友、role model——面前播放，你会自豪是好信号，说明你取了足够宽的视角。(01:02:55)：当你忙、在当下，很容易说「我就得做这一件大概不太好的事来完成这个。一旦做完会糟。但一旦做完就好。」然后你发现自己一次又一次一次又一次做它，不知不觉你失去了你想成为谁，你现在成了自己的 husk。所以我觉得那两块——leans in 你找到能量的地方、你特别找到能量的地方、你的超能力、你内在享受做的事——就确保它是你 actively 自豪的、那帮确保你不走一堆捷径。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those same lines, I think a lot of people have heard a version of this quote, which is, "New things that give you energy." So one, I love the additional piece of it is, "and that you're proud of." Two, you have another quote that I love that makes you think deeply about stuff, which is, "The secrets of life is things you've heard a million times already, you just weren't ready to hear them." Talk about that insight.
turns.zh: 类似地，我觉得很多人听过这引用的版本：「做给你能量的事。」一，我爱加的那块「你自豪的」。二，你有另一句我爱的引用让你深思：「生活的秘密是你听过一百万次的东西，只是你还没准备好听到。」聊聊这个洞察。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: So this I call the Hallmark card fallacy, which is you discover at great effort some deep insight that resonates with you and makes you see the world differently, and you want to share it. Insights are naturally viral. You want to share them and you go tell someone, it's like, "Guys, guys, the point of life is the friends we made along the way." And people go, "That's from a Hallmark card, man." And to you, it is you now possess the knowledge, the emotional intelligence to understand why that phrase has been shared so many times. Before, you heard it when you weren't ready and now it becomes a trite, "Duh, everyone says that. That can't possibly be a meaningful statement." (01:04:30): The reason people keep on saying it is because it's meaningful. And so I think that having that space of recognizing it, that when you have these epiphanies that come from different leaps in vertical development or the ability to, when you stare into the abyss and make it through the other side, you realize and learn a bunch of amazing things that you want to pass on others, and it's just really hard to get them to find it. (01:04:53): I find that that's one of the reasons I try to write things that are or share ideas that are like little seeds that you can shoot into someone's brain even if the soil's not ready for it, it's rocky or craggy, at some point in the future, if something goes through there and opens up a crack, that's sitting there to grow into an idea. One of the things that makes me the happiest is when someone I've mentored years and the years in the past, they go search me out years later and say, "Alex, I just want to let you know, you probably don't even remember talking to me, but that Tuesday at the building, the no-name cafe or whatever, on Google campus, you said something I was frustrated to hear in the moment I didn't understand it. And I just want to tell you, thank you because I finally understand what you were trying to tell me. And I realized that that influenced me in the decisions." That to me is one of those meaningful things I can hear. (01:05:41): And so I just find that you can't force it before people are ready to hear certain topics.
turns.zh: 这个我叫 Hallmark card 谬误。你花大力气发现某个让你共鸣、让你看世界不同的深度 insight，你想分享。Insight 天然 viral。你想分享，你告诉人说「大家大家，人生的意义是我们在路上交到的朋友。」大家说「哥们那是贺卡上的。」对你来说你现在拥有了理解为什么那句话被分享那么多次的情感智力知识。之前你在没准备好时听到，现在它变成 trite「啊大家都说。那不可能是 meaningful 的陈述。」(01:04:30)：大家一直说它的原因是它 meaningful。所以我觉得有那个空间认识它——当你有这些从 vertical development 不同 leap 来的 epiphany，或当你凝视深渊并走到另一边时，你学到一堆 amazing 的东西想传给别人，就是很难让他们找到它。(01:04:53)：我发现这是我试图写东西或分享 idea 的原因之一——像小种子射进某人脑子里，即使土壤还没准备好、 rocky 或 craggy，未来某个点如果有什么穿过那里打开一条缝，那个就在那里长成 idea。让我最开心的事之一是我多年前 mentor 过的人多年后 search 我出来说「Alex，我想让你知道，你可能都不记得和我聊过，但那个周二在 Google campus 的 no-name cafe，你说了什么我当时沮丧听到、不理解。我想说谢谢因为我终于理解你当时想告诉我什么。我意识到那个影响……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Man, that must feel so good to hear those sorts of closing the loop on something long ago. The point you make about cliches that you've heard a million times actually finally feeling right and profound, I had this very experience. I did a psychedelic trip with some friends a while ago, and at the end of it I was just like, "Man, love is all you need. Love is all you need." I felt that so deeply through the experience and I was telling people, they're like, "Shut up."
turns.zh: 天哪，那一定感觉很好，这种很久以前的事闭环。你关于 cliché 你听过一百万次终于感觉对和深刻，我有这个体验。我和朋友做了个 psychedelic trip，结束时我就想「天哪，爱就是你需要的一切。爱就是你需要的一切。」我通过那个体验深深感受到了，我告诉别人，他们说「闭嘴。」

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: You telling, oh, do you just do psychedelics? Yeah, it's funny.
turns.zh: 你告诉——哦你做 psychedelic？对，有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: I have a lot of folks in my broader space who obviously have used it. So I never personally have myself, but I find there's various ways. The transcendent mindset is this feeling of being part of something much, much, much larger than yourself and losing your ego in this thing. There's different ways of doing it. Some people will find it in hiking and being out in the wilderness alone. Some people find it being at a concert and thousands of people perfectly in sync to this thing. Some people find it in religious experience. Some people find it using psychedelics and others to help get there. But a lot of it, it's that same just being willing to be in awe. (01:06:53): There's so many times that people feel the feeling of awe or wonder or curiosity is treated as a not very serious or childlike thing. And I just don't get that because that is how you are open to disconfirming evidence. It's how you see beyond the current limits of what you... Your ego gets hurt when you get disconfirming evidence. You don't want to hear it. And so you'll construct the world around yourself to not get that disconfirming evidence. But disconfirming evidence is what makes systems strong. It's what makes you strong. And so how do you put yourself in the situation to get that information and really receive it? (01:07:28): And part of it is just coming in terms of the fact of early in my career, someone called me kooky a bit. Oh, man. I must be embarrassed. I'm like, "Okay, fine. Yeah, I'm kooky, whatever." I'm totally at peace with the idea that some people track me as kooky and not particularly serious. I think people who watch the work that I do and the indirect impact it has realize that I'm doing something that is working even if they don't fully understand how it works.
turns.zh: 我更广的空间里很多人显然用过。我自己从没做过，但我发现有各种方式。超越心态是这种作为比你大得多的东西的一部分、在其中失去 ego 的感觉。有不同方式。有人在徒步和独自在野外找到。有人在音乐会和几千人完美同步找到。有人在宗教体验里找到。有人用 psychedelic 找到。但很多是那个 same 愿意 in awe。(01:06:53)：有那么多时候人觉得 awe 或 wonder 或好奇的感觉被当作不很严肃或孩子气的东西。我就是不理解，因为那就是你对反驳证据保持开放的方式。是你看到超越当前极限的方式。你的 ego 在你得到反驳证据时受伤。你不想听。所以你围绕自己构建世界来 not 得到那个反驳证据。但反驳证据是让系统强大的。是让你强大的。所以你怎么把自己放在得到那个信息并真正接收它的情境里？(01:07:28)：部分是接受这个事实：我职业生涯早期有人说我有点 kooky。天哪。我得尴尬。我想「好吧，行。对，我 kooky，无所谓。」我完全平和于有些人 track 我为 kooky、不太严肃。我觉得看我做的事和间接影响的人 realize 我在做某种 work 的东西，即使他们不完全理解它怎么 work。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To start to close our conversation, I want to throw out one more seed that might land with someone in the right time. You have this concept of the adjacent possible, which I think is a really powerful concept. And it's basically argues that a lot of people jump to big bold ideas, and instead the better approach is think about what's a constraint you have and lean into the constraints and use that as a guide. Can you just talk about this and how this might inform how people think about product and strategy?
turns.zh: 为了开始收尾，我想再抛一个也许会在对的时间 land 的种子。你有相邻可能的概念，我觉得是很 powerful 的概念。它基本主张很多人跳到大胆 idea，而更好的 approach 是想你的约束是什么、leans in 约束、用它作 guide。聊聊这个以及它怎么 inform 人们想产品和战略？

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: Sure, yeah. The frame is the adjacent possible, which is I believe comes from design thinking. I've found it from designers in my life who are the ones who would just speak to it. And the adjacent possible is a set of actions that you do, that you can do. They are right in front of you that if you do them, they would work, almost certainly work. And in the tech industry in particular, we default assume that the adjacent possible is like this and then flying leap to something. And in reality, the adjacent possible is quite small. It's within arm's reach. And people will say, "Oh, you're being nihilist. You're limiting your potential. You're saying don't do big things." But when you recognize that your adjacent possible is relatively small, you realize that you actually have full agency to pick within the subset that is within your reach, and your actions matter because you take an action and now the world reconfigures and now you get a next set of actions and it's based partially on the action you just took. (01:09:11): And so if you slice this thing up and you have a coherent worldview and you have a principled approach, you can arc to wildly different outcomes than look like they were possible while at each point, each individual action is safe and reasonable. And so you can combine both of these things. I think so many times we try to jump and we jump to the end state of the thing. And actually you don't need to make that decision. If you can slice up your decisions into smaller and smaller decisions, I'm like, "This next step definitely makes sense." It will almost certainly pay for itself or the very least won't be too expensive. And then it might allow these other things to happen and you take it. And if those other things don't happen, okay, don't take another step on that path. That's fine. Go in other directions for a while. If it does, then take another step and another and another and another. (01:09:50): And this allows you to get rid of a lot of the risk and still be exposed to all the upside. And so the risk comes from trying to jump too far ahead in an unknown environment.
turns.zh: 当然。frame 是相邻可能，我相信来自设计思维。我是从生活中的设计师那里找到的。相邻可能是你做的一组行动，你能做的、就在你面前的，如果你做它们它们几乎确定会 work。在科技行业尤其，我们默认假设相邻可能是这样然后飞跃到某个东西。但现实里相邻可能相当小。在 arm 能达到的范围内。大家会说「哦你在虚无主义。你在限制你的潜力。你说别做大事。」但当你认识到你的相邻可能相对小，你 realize 你其实有完全的 agency 在你 reach 内的子集里 pick，你的行动 matter 因为你采取一个行动世界重新配置、现在你得到下一组行动、它部分基于你刚采取的行动。(01:09:11)：所以如果你把这个切片、你有连贯的世界观、你有原则性 approach，你可以 arc 到看起来可能却 wildly 不同的结果，同时在每个点每个个体行动都是安全合理的。所以你可以结合两者。我觉得很多时候我们试图跳、跳到东西的终态。其实你不需要做那个决策。如果你能把决策切成越来越小的决策——「这下一步 definitely 说得通。它几乎确定会回本或至少不会太贵。然后它可能允许这些其他事发生」——你做它。如果那些其他事没发生，好，不在那条路上再走一步。没关系。去别的方向一阵。如果发生了，再走一步、再一步、再一步。(01:09:50)：这让你去掉很多风险……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is the general advice if someone's working on trying to figure out the roadmap, trying to think about what products to build is the advice, don't be scared to go a little incremental versus what people are always pushed, to do bigger.
turns.zh: 大致建议是如果有人在想 figure out 路线图、想该 build 什么产品，建议是别怕做一点 incremental vs 大家总被推的做更大？

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: You need both. So if you only do incremental, you will follow the shortest, the steepest gradient in front of you. So UXR says a user wants to do this and you'll do exactly that and you'll end up random walking through the thing. So you need coherence about where you're going and the way you get that is by creating a North Star for yourself. It should be in three to five years in the future, it should be very low resolution. It should describe a thing that every single person who reads it who has any kind of knowledge that might be useful or relevant agrees that it is plausible. If this happens, I would not say, "Well, a miracle happened." It'd say, "I could see how that could work." And lawyers say, "I could see how that could work." And someone who's worked on this 30 years ago at a similar product that Microsoft says, "I can see how that could work." (01:10:51): And that if you got to the end point, everyone would high five because if it's going to be a thing, they're like, "I guess that could work." At the end we'd be like, "Oh yeah, neat." That's not worth it. You want another story would be like, "Yeah, great. Wow, we kick off. We changed the way this entire industry works," or whatever. And now this is your North Star. North Star should update, but it's because it's far off in the distance. It will update. It will slide up across the sky a little bit. It won't be jerking around. You'll be arcing slightly differently. And then what you do is you look in your adjacent possible and you look for the thing that has the steepest gradient that pulls you towards your North Star. So you just want to go in that direction and you want to go in this direction. This one is second most in demand from what you think, but it's pulling you the direction that you believe will pull you there. Go in that one. (01:11:31): And then they keep on repeating. That's it. But you need both. Because if you only do incremental, then you'll end up random walking into a corner. And if you only do the long-term, you end up dreaming big and designing castles in the sky that are impossible to actually manifest.
turns.zh: 两个都要。如果只做 incremental，你跟着面前最陡的梯度走。UXR 说用户想做这个你就做那个，你就 random walk。所以你需要 coherence 知道你去哪，通过给自己创造 North Star。它应该在 3 到 5 年后，非常低分辨率。它应该描述一个每个读它的、有相关知识的人都同意 plausible 的东西。如果这发生了，我不会说「奇迹发生了。」会说「我能看到它怎么 work。」律师说「我能看到它怎么 work。」30 年前在微软做类似产品的人说「我能看到它怎么 work。」(01:10:51)：而如果你到了终点，大家 high five 因为如果它是个事他们会「我猜那能 work」。到最后「哦对， neat。」那不值。你要另一个故事「对，great。哇我们改变了整个行业运作方式」之类的。这是你的 North Star。North Star 该更新，但因为它在远处，它会更新。它会在天上滑一点。不会 jerking。你会稍微不同地 arc。然后你看你的相邻可能、找有最陡梯度 pull 你朝 North Star 的那个。你就去那个方向。你去这个。这个第二多需求但 pull 你相信会 pull 你到那的方向。去那个。(01:11:31)：然后不断重复。就这样。但两个都要。因为如果只 incremental 你会 random walk 进角落。如果你只……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To give you a metaphor from an experience I had, I did this silent meditation retreat once, and a big part of Buddhism is to not cling to a specific outcome and not have a plan in mind and be sad if it doesn't work out. And so I asked them just how do you achieve success and want to be successful while not doing that? And their metaphor is point your card in a specific direction that you want to go. Just point your card in that direction, essentially in your example of North Star, and just start walking. Don't figure out this is exactly the path I'm going to take to get to this end destination.
turns.zh: 给个我从体验来的比喻：我做了一次静默冥想 retreat，佛教很大一部分是不执着于具体结果、不抱计划、不因没成而难过。所以我问他们怎么既成功又想成功又不做那个？他们的比喻是：把你的车指向你想去的方向。就指向那个方向——就是你的 North Star 例子——然后开始走。不要 figure out 这是我要走到那个终点的精确路径。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: Yeah. And you'll know after the fact, you'll say, "Oh, I curved a little bit or I had this little jog than there." And you'll say, "Ah, it would've been more efficient." But we're so focused on efficiency of not wasting effort that we ended up doing nothing at all or doing very dangerous things that don't work. So I'm much sure that I have a path that's slightly inefficient because we're navigating unknowns and we couldn't know no point. I think I've seen the number of times I find where people say, "I need to know for this strategy," that someone was trying to get me to look at and then say, "is this number in five years, is it going to be 93 or 95?" And it's like, I don't know. And it doesn't matter either if it's going to be that order of magnitude. (01:12:56): It doesn't matter, and we don't have to do that analysis if we believe that the order of magnitude is of that thing. It'd actually be we had spent all the time to get the illusion of precision, which at great expense, and then it's the people say, "Oh, I'm data-driven. I want to really run the analysis to ground." There's tons of stuff you can't know ahead of time. So if you're getting a false precision at the beginner, that's a comfort blanket. That's just helping you feel like there isn't uncertainty. There's uncertainty everywhere all the time. And trying to ignore it by trying to pin it down with fake numbers that you just made up for yourself at great expense is a really bad idea. And that's why if the ideas are strong enough, things that have a compounding return don't give you, "Oh, we'll either get 93 or 95." It's like, "We'll either get zero or we'll get 1,000." Great. It doesn't really matter if it's 1,000 or 1,001, who cares? It orders a magnitude larger than the alternative, and so it is better.
turns.zh: 对。你事后才知道「哦我弯了一点或我有个小 jog。」你说「啊，那会更高效。」但我们太 focus 于不浪费努力的高效以至于我们最后什么都不做或做不 work 的危险的事。所以我更 sure 我有一条稍微低效的路径因为我们在导航未知、我们没法知道。我觉得我看到很多次大家说「我需要为这个战略知道」某人试图让我看的，然后说「这个数字五年后是 93 还是 95？」就像我不知道。而且不重要如果是那个量级。(01:12:56)：不重要，我们不需要做那个分析如果我们相信那个东西的量级。其实如果我们花所有时间得到 precision 的错觉，很贵，然后大家说「哦我是数据驱动的。我要把分析做扎实。」有大量你没法事先知道的东西。所以如果你在开头得到 false precision，那是 comfort blanket。只是帮你感觉没有 uncertainty。到处都是 uncertainty 一直。试图通过用你编造的假数字 pin down 来忽略它是坏主意。所以如果 idea 够强、有复合回报的东西不会给你「哦我们要么 93 要么 95」。是「我们要么 0 要么 1000」。好。1000 还是 1001 真不重要谁在乎？它比替代品大量级大，所以更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really freeing. I noticed again, you were writing something. I'm again curious which you wrote down that you thought was insightful.
turns.zh: 那真释放。我注意到你又在写什么。我好奇你写下了什么你觉得有 insight 的。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: I actually this time I was not writing did something down. I was checking a thing I thought you might say that was going to reference was Tim Urban's, "Happiness is the reality minus expectations." I always get that backwards, but have you heard this frame, that happiness-
turns.zh: 我这次其实没写什么。我在查一个我以为你要提到的——Tim Urban 的「幸福是现实减期望」。我总搞反，但你听过这个 frame 吗，幸福——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's get into it. Yeah, we're not going to get this. This is great.
turns.zh: 来聊聊。对，我们不聊这个。这很好。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: "Happiness is reality minus expectations," and this is Tim Urban. It was from Wait But Why. And I think it's a very simple distillation of it, of if you set your expectations super high and it comes in and it's amazing, but it's below it, then it's a net negative. So the easiest thing, reality is hard to change. It's not impossible. It's hard to change. Your expectations are super easy. So just change your expectations. Hold it lightly and don't say, "Oh my gosh, this is going to be my kid's birthday. She's going to remember it. It's going to be the best birthday that she ever had and we're all it's going to be perfect." Because then when it doesn't go perfect and it starts raining that day, you're like, "Gosh." You get all worked up. Just say, "No, I want spend this day in a way that I can look back on and remember fondly." And that will include, yeah, it changed. (01:14:54): One other piece of advice someone gave me that I really like is try to feel the emotion about the story that'll make you feel in 10 years. So if it's funny in 10 years, try to see the humor in it now. And this one in particular was a friend, their newborn would, every time you changed her diaper, would poop. That was only... And when they did it, it would often be projectile. And so it was like a trap. You change the diaper. And it was like, what are you going to do in that situation? And then they're just like, "It's going to be a funny story in a few years, so let's see the humor in it now." Even though, God, I really wish this year-
turns.zh: 「幸福是现实减期望」，Tim Urban 的。来自 Wait But Why。我觉得是很简单的蒸馏：如果你设期望超高，结果 amazing 但低于它，那是净负。最简单的，现实难改。不是不可能。难。你的期望超容易。就改你的期望。轻持它，别说「天哪这是我孩子生日。她会记住。是她最好生日、我们都要完美。」因为当它不完美、那天下雨，你就「天哪」很 upset。就说「不，我想以能回头看、fondly 记住的方式过这一天。」那会包括，对，它变了。(01:14:54)：另一个有人给我的建议我很喜欢：试着感受那个会在 10 年后让你有感觉的情绪。如果 10 年后好笑，试现在看到幽默。这个具体是朋友，他们新生儿每次换尿布都拉。只有……而且做的时候经常是 projectile。所以像陷阱。你换尿布。那你能怎么办？他们就想「几年后这会是个好笑故事，所以现在就看到幽默。」即使天哪我真希望这年……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's funny.
turns.zh: 那很好笑。

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: ... you're not spraying poop on her. And I think that that kind of perspective is really, people sometimes hear this as, "Oh, you're saying don't dream big. Don't set high expectations. Don't expect more and be okay with mediocrity." That is not what I'm saying. I'm saying hold those expectations lightly. Allow them to change. Be willing to be convinced by different things, and seek something great. Seek something that you can be truly proud of and that feel very authentic to yourself if you achieved.
turns.zh: ……你别喷屎。我觉得那种 perspective 真的——大家有时听这个像「哦你说别梦想大。别设高期望。别期待更多、接受平庸。」那不是我在说。我在说轻持那些期望。允许它们变。愿意被不同东西说服，seek 伟大的东西。seek 你能真正自豪、感觉非常 authentic 于你如果达到的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Alex, I feel like I could talk to you for hours. I can't believe it's already been almost an hour and a half. So just to wrap things up, is there anything else that you thought would be fun to share or maybe a piece of wisdom you want to leave listeners with before we get to a very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: Alex，我觉得我能和你聊几个小时。不敢相信已经快一个半小时了。收尾前，还有什么你觉得好玩分享或想留给听众的智慧 piece 在我们到非常精彩的闪电问答前？

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: I think we covered it. I think we covered a lot of that. And again, we could go on for hours and hours and hours and hours. I could just do a random... I can feature The Compendium where I can pull up a random idea, and let's not do that.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们覆盖了。我觉得我们覆盖了很多那个。再说一次，我们可以聊几个小时几个小时。我可以就 random……我可以 feature The Compendium 拉一个随机 idea，但我们不做了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, amazing. Well, Alex, with that, we've reached the very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好，太好了。Alex，那我们到了非常精彩的闪电问答。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: I am ready.
turns.zh: 准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题。你最常推荐给人的两三本书？

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: Origin of Wealth by Eric Beinhocker, which is great. It's about a complexity economics, why the traditional economic model doesn't work, and also why it takes an evolutionary lens on what kinds of business plans work and how companies execute them. That I found my entree into a lot of the systems thinking and I thought it was just absolutely brilliant. And the other one is The Elements of Thinking in Systems, which is short, easy to read, very approachable. In fact, if anything, people think of it as not serious enough because it's too easy to read. It's one of those books that when you read at the beginning you'll say, "This sounds right." And then later, years later, if you read it again you'll go, "Oh my God, that was so... I wasn't ready for that yet, but that is totally the way." So she's one of the people who talks about dancing the systems. Let go and dance with the system is one of her lines, and I think it's just a phenomenal book.
turns.zh: Eric Beinhocker 的 Origin of Wealth，很好。关于复杂性经济学，为什么传统经济模型不 work，也用演化 lens 看什么样的商业计划 work、公司怎么执行。那是我进入很多系统思考的入口，我觉得绝对 brilliant。另一本是 The Elements of Thinking in Systems，短、易读、很 approachable。其实如果有什么，大家觉得它不够严肃因为太好读。它是那种你在开始读时会说「这听起来对」的书。然后几年后再读「天哪，那个太……我那时没准备好，但那 totally 是那个方式。」所以她是谈论与系统共舞的人之一。放手与系统共舞是她的 line 之一，我觉得是 phenomenal 的书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next question. Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 下一个问题。你有最近最喜欢的电影或剧集吗？

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: For me, I was thinking about this, it's The Green Knight, which I watched I think a few years old. It's about the Arthurian legend. It's a challenging movie. In fact, when I watched it, I was like, "I dislike this. I do not find this interesting." And then I couldn't stop thinking about it and it helped me. I think this is one of the reasons I like to write in parable is a parable is open-ended. It encourages and requires the listener to engage into the idea and play with it and see how it affects them and how they affect it. And so for me, The Green Knight, again, I'm not excited to watch it again, but I found it to be the most impactful movie I've seen in the last couple of years in terms of amount of thinking that it caused me to do afterwards.
turns.zh: 对我来说，我想了想，是 The Green Knight，几年前的。关于亚瑟王传说。是有挑战性的电影。其实我看时觉得「我不喜欢这个。我觉得这没意思。」然后我停不下来想它，它帮了我。我觉得这是我喜欢用寓言写的原因之一——寓言是开放结尾的。它鼓励并要求听者 engage 进 idea、玩它、看它怎么影响他们、他们怎么影响它。所以对我来说 The Green Knight——我不是兴奋再看一遍——但我发现它是过去几年对我影响最大的电影，就它让我事后思考的量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that says a lot. Next question, do you have a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 哇，那说了很多。下一个问题。你有最近发现的、很爱的产品吗？

turns.speaker: Alex Komoroske
turns.en: To me, I think the answer for me is WebSim. It's the one that I like playing around with a lot. And I've said it before, I use Claude 20 times a day. I find that it's almost impossible for me to imagine doing work. I mean of course now I've got to use Strawberry and see how that feels, but yeah.
turns.zh: 对我来说我觉得答案是 WebSim。是我喜欢玩的。我说过，我一天用 Claude 20 次。我发现几乎没法想象做工作。当然现在我得用 Strawberry 看看感觉如何，但对。

turns.speaker: Lenny

Just one quick framing. To me, if you ask somebody on the street to tell you what the canonical piece of software is, the answer they'll give you is something like Instagram, which is to say an app, which I think is a shame because an app is monolithic. It's one size fits all. It's not decomposable. It doesn't meaningfully interact with anything else in the broader ecosystem. And it's also only allowed to exist if some of the largest companies in the world say it may exist, which is insane to me. (01:21:26): To me, software is alchemy. It's the ability to extend human agency beyond ourselves to create something that can then combine with what others have created in unexpected and unforeseen ways to create this commentary of possibility of human agency. And somehow in the past decade, we've become convinced that all of this potential should be squeezed into about a dozen little boxes on your phone. And now with the power of AI, everyone just is default assuming that what's going to happen is we're all going to be locked inside of a box with a super God AI Clippy. And the only thing that people disagree about is which Clippy is it going to be? Whose Clippy is it going to be? (01:21:57): That to me is bonkers. I don't want that world at all. I want a world where we use this magical duct tape to escape the box, to allow software and humans using it to lean into their agency. And so for me, one of the reasons I'm excited about LLMs being a disruptive technology is I think that it allows us to get out of this monolithic sense of whatever. We're all just beholden to a decreasing number, very powerful organizations, and lean into everybody being able to be creative and collaborative and exercise their agency in a pro-social way.
